metadata.title: Claude, Session Report.
metadata.subtitle: The Script Counts, Claude Explains
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Teardown register: when Claude hands you a session report full of exact numbers, is Claude the one doing the counting? Takes the skill apart — the script that tallies, the template that moves, the model that reads and explains — and lands the carry-out that counting and explaining are two different jobs.
metadata.anchor_pair: B03 -> B06 (/tmp/session-report.json: planted as the script's output, then returned to as the untouched middleman)

beats.narration_text: Here's the mistake — thinking the session-report skill counts your tokens itself. It doesn't. A bundled script does the counting. Claude just reads the results. So what's actually there?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'Does session-report count every token itself?', hesitates on 'count', corrects to 'read', lands the real question

beats.narration_text: Here's what it sounds like from the outside: Claude has a session-report skill, and every number on the page — tokens, cache hits, subagent calls — feels like Claude tallied it in its head. That's the natural read of what a skill is. It's also wrong.

shot.new_visual_element: SOUNDS LIKE CLAUDE DID THE COUNTING

production_viz.label: SOUNDS LIKE CLAUDE DID THE COUNTING
production_viz.caption: that's the natural read

beats.narration_text: Here's the test: delete analyze-sessions.mjs from the skill folder. The report doesn't degrade — it can't run at all. Nothing else inside this skill knows how to count. The counting was never Claude's job; it lives in that one file, and the whole thing dies without it.

shot.new_visual_element: DELETE THE SCRIPT, THE REPORT IS GONE

production_viz.label: DELETE THE SCRIPT, THE REPORT IS GONE
production_viz.caption: the counting was never Claude's

beats.narration_text: Here's what actually does the counting: analyze-sessions.mjs. It walks your raw session data, tallies every number, and writes one answer — slash tmp slash session-report dot json — before Claude ever opens the report. Numbers first, on disk, already computed.

Claude's real job starts after that file exists: open the json, skim the totals — overall usage, by project, by subagent, by skill — and decide which numbers actually deserve explaining. That's editorial work, not arithmetic.

The report's interactive pieces — sorting a table, expanding a row, drawing a bar out of ASCII characters — already live in a template file Claude copies in. They chose to hand-code the interactions once, in the template, so Claude never writes markup. Its job on top is the numbers and the narrative, not the sorting code.

production_viz.label: THE TEMPLATE ALREADY MOVES
production_viz.caption: Claude's job is words, not markup

beats.narration_text: So that json file — the one the script wrote before any of this started — is still sitting inside the finished report, untouched. Every number on the page traces straight back to it, not to Claude's reasoning.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — SAME FILE, UNCHANGED

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — SAME FILE, UNCHANGED
production_viz.caption: every number traces back to it

beats.narration_text: Here's the interesting trade-off. A report that looks right doesn't prove Claude read every line of your session logs — it read one script's summary. And a report that looks wrong doesn't prove Claude reasoned badly — the script may have computed something you didn't expect, and Claude relayed it faithfully. Neither outcome is proof of the thing you probably think it's proving.
So here's what a session report actually is: not Claude counting your tokens — a script that counts, and Claude that explains what the count means. Two different jobs, one file between them.

props.quote: A session report isn't Claude counting your tokens — it's a script that counts, and Claude that explains what the count means.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt — paste it into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini. I want to understand which parts of a task belong to a deterministic script and which parts belong to a language model. Pick one recurring task in your work that involves both crunching data and explaining it — a weekly metrics email, a support-ticket summary, a bill-of-materials review. Ask the model to walk you through how to split it: the exact numbers a script should compute, the shape they should be in, and what the model should say about them that the script cannot. Go deeper: what happens to the explanation when the script is wrong, and how would you design the split so the model's job is verifiable, not just plausible? Liam, in for Bear.

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to understand which parts of a task belong to a deterministic script and which parts benefit from a language model. Here is one recurring task in my work that involves both crunching data and explaining it: [describe one task you do at least weekly — a metrics email, a support-ticket summary, a code-review digest, a bill-of-materials, whatever fits]. Walk me through how you would split it into two jobs: (1) the exact quantities a script should compute and the shape they should be written in — field names, types, groupings; (2) what the language model should say about those quantities that the script cannot — the framing, the trade-offs, what to flag, what to ignore. Show me the split as a small JSON schema for the script's output plus a short example of the explanation the model would write on top.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: what happens to the explanation when the script is wrong — does the model catch it, hide it, or amplify it? How would you design the split so the model's job is verifiable against the script's output, not just plausible on its face?
